title: Microservices Reference
description: A quick reminder of the ideas and examples in the Microservices lessons. Open the linked lesson when you need more help.

entries.name: Small services with clear jobs
entries.summary: A service is a part that does work for another part. Microservices divide an app by jobs, such as catalog search and lending.

example.code:
Catalog service: book titles and authors
Loan service: who borrowed each copy
Browser: shows results to a learner

notes: Many tiny services can be harder to manage than one clear application.

entries.name: Own the data you change
entries.summary: A service should clearly own the data it changes. Other services use its interface rather than editing its tables directly.

example.code:
Catalog owns Book records
Loans owns Loan records
Loans asks Catalog whether book 17 exists

notes: Shared writable tables create hidden links between services.

entries.name: Contracts explain requests
entries.summary: A contract describes the request fields and response fields. Both sides need to agree on their meaning.
notes: Do not change a field meaning without telling callers.

entries.name: Direct calls can wait
entries.summary: In a direct call, the caller waits for a reply. This is simple to follow but the caller depends on the other service responding.

example.code:
Loans -> Catalog: is book 17 known?
Catalog -> Loans: yes
Loans continues

notes: Always plan for slow or missing replies.

entries.name: Events announce something happened
entries.summary: An event reports a past fact. Other services may react to it without the sender waiting for every reaction.

example.code:
Event: BookBorrowed
Fields: eventId=81, copyId=203
Report service updates a daily count

notes: Choose names that describe a fact, not a vague request.

entries.name: Duplicate messages are possible
entries.summary: Message delivery can repeat. A consumer should recognise an event it has already handled.

example.code:
Receive event 81: increase count; remember 81
Receive event 81 again: ignore duplicate
Count increases once

notes: Do not assume every event arrives exactly once.

entries.name: Timeouts bound waiting
entries.summary: A timeout sets a limit on waiting. The caller must choose a useful response when that limit passes.

example.code:
Request begins at 0 ms
Timeout limit: 800 ms
No reply at 800 ms -> show a retry message

notes: A timeout does not cancel all work in another service automatically.

entries.name: Circuit breakers pause failing calls
entries.summary: A circuit breaker stops repeated calls to a service that is failing. Later it allows a small trial to see whether recovery happened.

example.code:
Several Catalog calls fail
Breaker opens: new calls fail fast
After a pause: allow one trial call

notes: A circuit breaker does not repair the failed service.

entries.name: Work across services needs recovery
entries.summary: A multi-step business action can partly succeed. A recovery action, often called compensation, tries to undo an earlier step.

example.code:
1. Reserve a book copy
2. Record the loan
If step 2 fails: release the reservation

notes: Do not assume several services share one automatic database transaction.

entries.name: Versions protect callers
entries.summary: A new contract version gives callers time to move. A safe added optional field is often easier than removing a field callers still need.
notes: Adding a field can still break strict callers; check their contracts.

entries.name: Trace a request across parts
entries.summary: A trace follows one request through several services. A shared trace ID connects the records.

example.code:
trace-7 Browser -> Catalog
trace-7 Catalog -> Search index
trace-7 Search index took 900 ms

notes: Unrelated log lines are hard to join without a shared ID.

entries.name: Choose services only when needed
entries.summary: Microservices bring independent releases and scaling, but add network calls and more operations work. Compare those costs before splitting an app.

example.code:
Small team, one release schedule -> one well-organised app
Many teams, different scaling needs -> consider service boundaries

notes: Do not turn a static tutorial website into a backend project just to practise architecture.
